subject: Renewal: Dedicated capacity top-up and overflow fallback
messages:
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
To: Sarah Jenkins <sarah.jenkins@cobalthealth.com>
Cc: Tom Reyes <tom.reyes@cobalthealth.com>
Date: Mon, 1 Feb 2027 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Renewal planning — capacity add-on options & overflow behavior

Sarah —

As Cobalt’s renewal approaches next month I wanted to outline a couple of pragmatic options for expanding your Dedicated pool and how overflow would behave if you hit the reserved ceiling. The objective is to avoid surprises in latency while keeping spend predictable. Short summary: two approaches we see work well in practice.

Option A (soft cap + on-demand overflow):
- Add X reserved GPUs to raise baseline throughput.
- When baseline is exhausted, requests spill to on-demand instances at our hosted rate + 20% premium.
- Optional daily spend cap to stop runaway cost.

Option B (hard cap + queueing/failover):
- Strict ceiling on reserved GPUs; additional requests are queued or rejected.
- We can route failed requests to a lower-cost, smaller-context model as a graceful degradation option.

To make a concrete proposal I need: desired baseline throughput (rps), tolerance for degraded responses, and whether procurement needs an annual committed spend vs monthly billing. I’ve attached a short worksheet to map throughput to GPU counts and an initial renewal addendum draft.

I’ll loop in Laura and Dev to validate the performance numbers.

Next steps: if you can share target baseline and a preferred overflow behavior I’ll draft terms you can share with procurement.

—Ben
Ben Carter
Enterprise Account Executive, Redwood Inference
Attach: SLA_throughput_worksheet.xlsx (spreadsheet)
Attach: renewal_addendum_draft.pdf (doc)

From: Sarah Jenkins <sarah.jenkins@cobalthealth.com>

Date: Wed, 3 Feb 2027 10:24:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Renewal planning — capacity add-on options & overflow behavior

Ben —

Thanks for the clear options. A couple constraints from our side:
- We cannot accept open-ended overage without a hard monthly cap. IT will not sign off on potentially unlimited hosted spend.
- Our primary driver is stable latency for inference-heavy batches (peak windows during mornings). Baseline throughput target is ~450 rps sustained and occasional spikes to ~750 rps for 20–30 minutes.
- Procurement prefers annual commit but we can consider a quarterly review cadence.

Given the above, our preference is a soft-cap approach only if we can attach a strict daily/monthly spend cap on overflow. If not possible, we prefer a hard cap + automatic fallback to a smaller model (we can accept a mild quality regression for fallback requests).

Also looping Tom in from ops to confirm whether degraded results are acceptable during spikes.

—Sarah
Sarah Jenkins
Director, ML Platforms — Cobalt Health

From: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
To: Sarah Jenkins <sarah.jenkins@cobalthealth.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>, Tom Reyes <tom.reyes@cobalthealth.com>

Subject: Re: Renewal planning — capacity add-on options & overflow behavior

Hi all —

Quick feasibility check from the solutions side after reviewing the worksheet Ben attached. High level recommendations:

1) Baseline sizing
- 12x A100-ish slots (reserved) maps to ~500 rps for your typical prompt mix (we tested with ~1.2k token avg).

2) Overflow handling choices and trade-offs
- Soft-cap + on-demand overflow: straightforward to implement. We can gate overflow with a configurable daily spend cap (we’ve implemented $/day and $/month alarms and hard stops for other customers). On-demand instances will start within region and can add the additional capacity quickly but there is a small cold-start window for very large scale — expect a 10–30s tail in the first minute of a major spike.

- Hard-cap + queued/fallback responses: lowest predictable spend. We can implement a prioritized queue with a max wait and automatic fallback to a smaller model (lower VRAM) for time-sensitive requests. That avoids on-demand costs but trades off quality and sometimes latency.

3) Suggested contract language (short):
- Baseline: 12 reserved GPUs; guaranteed baseline throughput of 500 rps (95th pct).
- Overflow: soft-cap enabled; overflow to Hosted at standard hosted rate + 20% premium; daily hard-stop at $6,000 (customer can choose to disable stop and accept billing).
- Fallback option: if customer opts out of overflow billing, traffic will be degraded via fallback model with agreed SLO for quality.

I’ve attached a tuned worksheet and a redline-friendly addendum. If these figures look close we can convert to a formal amendment for procurement.

—Laura
Laura Bennett
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Laura / Ben —

Thanks for the options. A few operational clarifications from our side:
- The daily hard-stop is mandatory for finance approval. The $6,000 number you proposed is a good starting point; procurement will ask to model what that means for a quarter.
- For fallback, degradation is acceptable only if we can control which request classes get degraded (e.g., background batch jobs OK to degrade; interactive clinical decision endpoints must always be served or queued). Can you add an option in the routing rules to tag routes/paths as 'no-degrade'?

Also: can you confirm whether KV cache priming persists across on-demand spill instances, or whether those instances will have cold caches that affect latency?

Tom

From: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>
To: Tom Reyes <tom.reyes@cobalthealth.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>

Date: Tue, 9 Feb 2027 16:20:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Renewal planning — capacity add-on options & overflow behavior

Tom / Sarah / Ben —

Technical confirmations inline:
- KV cache: on-demand spill instances will start without your reserved pool's warmed KV cache. We provide two mitigations: prefix caching replication (best-effort sync to new instances for hot prefixes) and a short-lived warmup path that primes the cache using replayed recent traffic; neither is perfect but both reduce the cold-cache penalty. Expect 5–15% latency hit on the first few thousand tokens served by a newly provisioned on-demand instance.

- Routing: we can support route tags like 'no-degrade' and enforce hard routing (reject or queue) for those routes. Others can be allowed to overflow/fallback to smaller models. This is configurable per-customer and per-route.

- Billing/control: we will include a daily hard-stop at $6,000 for overflow charges in the addendum. If the stop triggers we will (a) pause overflow to hosted; (b) optionally enable fallback routing for non-critical paths if you choose.

Next operational steps: Ben — if Cobalt accepts the 12 GPUs / 500 rps baseline + soft-cap with $6k daily stop we’ll produce a final addendum for signature and add a configuration ticket for route tagging and cache-prime scripts.

—Dev
Dev Patel
Engineering Manager, Runtime — Redwood Inference
